channel.title: Robotics & AI Daily Briefing
channel.description: New cs.RO and cs.AI papers, bucketed and summarized every arXiv announcement day

item.title: Today's most useful results come from better controls and readouts, not bigger models: a scripted retreat matches a learned VLA corrector, reading logits beats a fine-tuned emotion model, and robots that read human actions help about as well as robots that are told what to do.
item.description:
Today's most useful results come from better controls and readouts, not bigger models: a scripted retreat matches a learned VLA corrector, reading logits beats a fine-tuned emotion model, and robots that read human actions help about as well as robots that are told what to do.
Several papers today show that how something is measured or read out changes the conclusion more than the model does: a paired placebo shrinks the value of a learned VLA corrector, a logit readout turns 'VLMs fail at fine-grained emotion' into 'VLMs beat the fine-tuned model', and a compact policy matches systems 40-160x larger once its visual encoder is controlled. On the HRI side, assistance is increasingly triggered by what the person does (an action's outcome, a hand pose, a push on a carried load) rather than by an explicit instruction, while LLM-driven robots become easier to supervise when their plans are exposed as typed, structured commitments. In manipulation, contact feedback is being added to vision-first policies through the cheapest available channel, and a growing runtime layer decides how much of a frozen policy's action chunk to trust. World models keep showing the same gap: video that looks right while actions, hidden objects or unstable modes are wrong. For a team building interactive robots, the common thread is to test the specific property you rely on (the human cue, the contact event, the occluded object) with a control condition, before adding learned machinery.

item.title: Social robots are starting to plan how loud, fast and expressive they are, while new probes show VLAs often ignore what the person actually asked.
item.description:
Social robots are starting to plan how loud, fast and expressive they are, while new probes show VLAs often ignore what the person actually asked.
Several papers today treat social behaviour as something the robot actively produces: footstep noise, gesture timing, facial expression and execution speed are planned outputs, not side effects. A second group treats the human as a physical partner with their own forces, fatigue and fragility rather than as an obstacle or a remote operator. At the same time, diagnostic work on VLAs shows that nominal task success hides weak instruction following: policies grab the object the scene suggests, and safety refusals learned in text do not carry over to actions or grounding outputs. The practical consequence for an HRI team is that interaction quality has to be measured channel by channel, and that 'does the robot do what this person asked, and refuse what it should' needs its own tests. Much of the remaining engineering work fixes frozen policies at execution time, which is where a deployment team can act today.
